content: Brachial plexus injury (BPI) refers to damage to the brachial plexus, a network of nerves that originates from the spinal cord between the fifth cervical vertebra (C5) and the first thoracic vertebra (T1). This nerve network extends through the neck, the axilla (armpit), and into the arm, providing motor and sensory innervation to the upper limb. BPI can lead to significant functional impairment in one or, in rare cases, both upper limbs. This loss of function can severely impact an individual’s ability to perform daily activities, potentially resulting in economic difficulties, psychological distress such as depression, and, in extreme cases, challenges to basic survival. The first recorded description of an obstetric brachial plexus injury was made by Smellie in 1764. In 1872, Duchenne identified traction as a cause of BPI. Subsequently, Erb proposed that traction or compression of the C5 and C6 nerve roots could also result in BPI. In 1900, Thourborn became the first scientist to publish an article on the direct repair of brachial plexus components. By 1903, Harris and Low had reported the first cases of neurotization, a surgical technique involving nerve transfer. In 1920, Vulpius and Stoffel pioneered the re-routing of fascicles from the pectoral nerves to the musculocutaneous and axillary nerves. In 1947, Seddon introduced a method for surgically addressing traction injuries using long interpositional nerve grafts, which was subsequently published. However, in 1966, during a meeting of the International Society of Orthopedic Surgery and Traumatology (SICOT) in Paris, it was concluded that surgical repair of BPI was nearly impossible. Despite this, Stevens later provided a detailed explanation of the biomechanics of traction injuries affecting the upper limb and neck, as well as their impact on the brachial plexus. Over time, significant advancements were made in the field of BPI treatment. Pioneers such as Narakas, Millesi, Allieu, Brunelli, Gu, Terzis, and Doi successfully introduced microsurgical techniques for nerve repair and regeneration, revolutionizing the management of brachial plexus injuries.
